headline: India shrugs off Wall Street's AI rout; Tata Steel's big APL Apollo deal

segments.title: The big picture
segments.script:
Good morning. It's Monday, the twenty-third of November, and this is your Market Brief.

Three things matter most today. First, Wall Street had its roughest week in years. The Nasdaq fell more than 5 percent on Friday alone, and the S and P 500 and the Dow both slipped into correction, after Anthropic's much-awaited market debut failed to lift the AI trade. Asian markets are falling hard again this morning, with Korea's Kospi down as much as five and a half percent.

Second, India is standing apart, at least for now. The Nifty has just notched a fourth straight weekly gain, at nine-month highs, carried by foreign buying, softer crude and a rally in banks. GIFT Nifty is pointing to a gap-up start of more than 150 points, and it's monthly expiry day.

Third, a big deal in steel. Tata Steel plans to buy more than a quarter of APL Apollo Tubes for around 15,500 crore rupees, in a set of transactions that reshapes the steel tubes business. More on all of that in a moment.

segments.title: How markets closed
segments.script:
Now to how markets closed. The Nifty ended Friday at 25,800.6, capping a gain of about 2.2 percent for the week. That's its fourth winning week in a row, the longest streak in five months. Banks and financials did the heavy lifting, and the Nifty Bank hit a milestone of its own. The broader market, and metal and IT stocks, lagged as global volatility rose.

The driving force has been money from abroad. Analysts say sustained buying by foreign institutional investors, a recovering rupee and softer crude have put Indian shares on a firmer footing. The Nifty has rallied about 14 percent in four weeks.

For this morning, GIFT Nifty futures were around 25,912 just before eight, indicating a positive open as US futures bounce. But weakness across Asia, and today's monthly derivatives expiry, could keep a lid on enthusiasm.

The levels analysts are watching: 26,000 is the immediate hurdle. A sustained move above it, they say, could bring a fresh attempt at the record high of 26,373. On the downside, support is seen in the 25,500 to 25,600 zone, and then at 25,300.

One date for your calendar. Markets are shut tomorrow, Tuesday, for Guru Nanak Jayanti, so it's a four-day trading week. Today also brings the HSBC flash purchasing managers' index for November.

Not everyone is convinced by the rally. Veteran investor Shankar Sharma calls the large-cap rally a bear market move, a countertrend bounce, and says foreign buying reflects tactical shifts rather than renewed faith in India. Raghvendra Nath of Ladderup Asset Managers, on the other hand, expects foreign money to keep coming in as long as the AI trade stays volatile, though he warns December quarter results may not match the September quarter.

segments.title: IPOs and deals
segments.script:
Now to IPOs and deals, and the big one first. Tata Steel plans to buy a 26.38 percent stake in APL Apollo Tubes for about 15,511 crore rupees, and make an open offer for another 26 percent. It will also transfer its tubes and pipes business to APL Apollo, and sell it Tata Steel Colors, in deals worth up to 28,000 crore rupees combined. Both stocks will be in focus this morning.

In the primary market, a couple of companies are trimming their plans. Medicap Healthcare, which makes pharmaceutical closures in Vadodara, has cut its IPO size by 29 percent to 170 crore rupees and dropped its pre-IPO placement. Passenger mobility company Chartered Speed has cut its issue to 433 crore rupees after SEBI's regulatory changes, with a fresh issue of 333 crore and an offer for sale of 100 crore.

Infrastructure investment trusts are lining up too. Investment bankers say four to five privately placed trusts could go public by March 2027, raising about 17,000 crore rupees together. Brookfield-backed Altius Telecom Infrastructure Trust has filed for a possible 6,000 crore rupee issue.

And one global note. Anthropic's blockbuster listing in the US earned Wall Street banks more than 500 million dollars in fees, though some bankers complained about compressed deadlines and unusual restrictions.

segments.title: Economy and policy
segments.script:
Now to the economy and policy. India's eight core industries grew 10.9 percent in October, a 31-month high. Coal output jumped 23 percent and electricity generation nearly 22 percent, against a weak base a year ago, when both had contracted.

The cost of oil is biting, though. India's net oil and gas import bill rose 60 percent in October from a year earlier, to 16 billion dollars, as Brent crude averaged nearly double its level of a year ago. Cooking gas consumption fell more than 12 percent. For April to October, the net import bill reached 97.7 billion dollars, against 70.3 billion a year earlier.

On trade, India and the European Union are likely to sign their long-awaited free trade agreement on the sixteenth of December in Brussels. Negotiations concluded in January, after more than two decades of talks, and 93 percent of Indian shipments are set to get duty-free access to the bloc. Engineering exports jumped 36 percent in October to 12.74 billion dollars, led by strong US demand. Meanwhile, the Centre is working to resolve a deadlock over Scotch whisky from the UK, after revenue intelligence officials applied an effective duty of 162.5 percent on bulk imports.

On the rupee, the Chief Economic Adviser said India may have to manage rupee strength, not weakness, next financial year, with several agencies expecting Brent to fall below 80 dollars a barrel. Analysts quoted by Mint caution that record foreign inflows shouldn't be read as a fundamental shift in how foreign investors see India.

A strong set of numbers from state-run lenders. Public sector banks posted their highest-ever net profit, 1.09 lakh crore rupees, in the first half of this financial year, with their capital adequacy ratio improving to 16.89 percent.

From Prime Minister Modi, a pointed challenge to India Inc. After tax cuts and trade deals, he asked industry whether it had raised wages and created jobs, and urged companies to cut import dependence and invest in new sectors.

And the Budget wish lists are arriving. Non-bank lenders want a dedicated fund for lending to small businesses, run by the Small Industries Development Bank, while aluminium makers want the customs duty on primary aluminium cut from 7.5 percent to zero.

segments.title: Around the world
segments.script:
Now around the world. Friday on Wall Street was brutal. The Dow fell 1.9 percent, the S and P 500 fell 3.7 percent, and the Nasdaq lost 5.3 percent, capping its worst week since March 2020. Worries over AI valuations, funding costs and data centre spending are unwinding the trade that powered this year's rally. This morning, though, Nasdaq futures are up nearly 3 percent and S and P futures more than 2 percent.

Asia isn't getting that relief yet. Korea's Kospi fell as much as five and a half percent, with Samsung and SK Hynix both down more than 4 percent. Regulators are rushing in. South Korea is preparing a market stabilisation fund, Taiwan has banned short selling below the previous close after its worst week in 35 years, and China's state-backed funds bought a record amount of exchange-traded funds on Friday. China will also cut the margin requirement for buying stocks with borrowed money to 80 percent, from the thirtieth of November.

Oil is a touch softer. Brent was around 92 dollars a barrel this morning, down about a third of a percent, with attacks in the Iran war limiting the losses. US bond yields have eased below 5 percent, and the dollar is just off a 19-month high.

As for the Federal Reserve, a Wall Street Journal report carried by Mint says it is almost certain to raise interest rates next month to cool inflation, but the size of the increase is anyone's guess. This week brings US growth figures and the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, in a week shortened by Thanksgiving.

segments.title: Your money
segments.script:
Now to your money, starting with gold. Gold has had its biggest weekly drop in eight months, sliding to its lowest since September 2025 and slipping below 4,000 dollars an ounce, while silver crashed nearly 4 percent. Rate-hike expectations in the US, a stronger dollar and fears of slower AI spending are weighing on metals. Gold is now nearly 24 percent below its August peak, which is some relief for families shopping ahead of the wedding season. This morning it has bounced, as the tech rout sends traders towards safe havens. Experts quoted by Mint say investors should focus on allocation and staggered buying.

A useful tax ruling. The Delhi bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal quashed reassessment proceedings against a retired Delhi Transport Corporation employee, because the mandatory notice was sent to his former office address and not properly served on him.

And from the Supreme Court, retirement benefits can't be held up by a pending appeal. It upheld the release of 33.95 lakh rupees in gratuity to two retired Delhi Development Authority employees who had been acquitted in a corruption case.

On loans, Karur Vysya Bank has raised its marginal cost of funds based lending rate by 5 basis points across tenures, taking the one-year rate to 9.30 percent, while cutting its base rate by 25 basis points.

For provident fund members, the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation is working on a systematic withdrawal plan that would let retiring members draw their savings monthly, quarterly or half-yearly. And a reminder that a partial provident fund withdrawal for buying a house is tax-exempt once you have five years of service.

Two warnings for investors. Delhi Police has arrested seven people across five states over a 67.78 lakh rupee fraud run through fake trading platforms and WhatsApp groups. And in Jodhpur, investigators found rhenium mixed into gold that carried a 22-carat hallmark, raising questions about purity testing.

That's the brief. Today, watch whether the Nifty can clear 26,000 on expiry day, how Tata Steel and APL Apollo trade on their big deal, the flash purchasing managers' numbers, and whether Asia's slide eases as US futures recover. Markets are closed tomorrow for Guru Nanak Jayanti. Have a good Monday.
